''intermedia'' | ''Angophora ochrophylla'' R.T.Baker | ''Eucalyptus florida'' Brooker | ''Metrosideros floribunda'' Sm. }} }} '''''Angophora floribunda''''', commonly known as the '''rough-barked apple''', is a common woodland and forest tree of the family [[Myrtaceae]] native to Eastern Australia. Reaching 30 m (100 ft) high, it is a large tree with fibrous bark and cream-white flowers that appear over the Austral summer. It grows on alluvial soils on floodplains and along watercourses. Much of the land it grew on has been cleared for agriculture. ==Description== [[File:Angophora floribunda in flower.jpg|thumb|''Angophora floribunda'' in flower,
Port Hacking, December]] ''Angophora floribunda'' is a large, wide, spreading tree growing to a height of 30 m (100 ft). The trunk is often gnarled and crooked with fibrous grey bark.{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Angophora |species=floribunda|author=Hill, Ken}} Like all members of the genus ''Angophora'', the dull to glossy green leaves are arranged oppositely along the stem. 5.5 to 15 cm (2.2–6 in) long and 1–5 cm (0.4–2 in) wide. They are [[Glossary of leaf morphology#lanceolate|lanceolate]] to ovate and attached to the stems by 0.6–1.5 cm (0.2–0.6 in) long [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]]. The leaves in the western parts of the range are narrower than those in more coastal regions. The cream-white flowers appear from November to March. It can be confused with ''A. subvelutina'', but the latter has leaves that are heart-shaped at their base and lacking petioles, arise from the stem.{{cite book |author1=Fairley, Alan |author2=Moore, Philip |title=Native Plants of the Sydney District:An Identification Guide |year=2000 |edition= 2nd|publisher=Kangaroo Press |page=195|location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-7318-1031-7}} ==Taxonomy== The rough-barked apple was described by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] in 1797 as ''Metrosideros floribunda'', having been collected by Surgeon-General of New South Wales, [[John White (surgeon)|John White]] in 1794. It was growing from seed in Empress Josephine's arboretum at [[Château de Malmaison|Malmaison]] by 1804, when [[Étienne Pierre Ventenat]] catalogued it in his ''Jardin de la Malmaison''.{{APNI | name = ''Metrosideros floribunda'' Sm. | id = 56742}} The species name is derived from the [[Latin]] ''floribunda'' 'abundant flowers'.{{cite book |author1=Elliot, Rodger W. |author2=Jones, David L. |author3=Blake, Trevor |title=Encyclopaedia of Australian Plants Suitable for Cultivation: Vol. 2|year=1985|page=196 |publisher=Lothian Press |location=Port Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-143-5}} [[Robert Sweet (botanist)|Robert Sweet]] gave it its current name in 1830.{{APNI | name = ''Angophora floribunda'' (Sm.) Sweet | id = 37795}} Common names include rough-barked apple, apple box, rusty gum, gum myrtle and Boondah. Genetic work has been published showing ''Angophora'' to be more closely related to ''Eucalyptus'' than ''[[Corymbia]]'', and in 2000 botanist Ian Brooker coined the name ''Eucalyptus florida'' for this species as ''Eucalyptus floribunda'' and ''E. intermedia'' had already been used for other eucalypts.{{Cite journal | last1 = Brooker | first1 = M. I. H. |title=A new classification of the genus ''Eucalyptus'' L'Hér. (Myrtaceae)| journal = Australian Systematic Botany | volume = 13 | pages = 79–148 | doi = 10.1071/SB98008 | year = 2000 | issue = 1 | bibcode = 2000AuSyB..13...79B }} This tree hybridises with the broad-leaved apple (''[[Angophora subvelutina]]'').{{cite journal |last=Benson |first=Doug |author2=McDougall, Lyn |year=1998|title=Ecology of Sydney plant species:Part 6 Dicotyledon family Myrtaceae |journal=Cunninghamia |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=809–987 |url=http://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0008/58049/Cun5Ben808.pdf}} Genetic analysis suggests the two might be a single species, despite their different morphology. Hybridization is present in some populations where both taxa occur but not others.{{cite journal |last1=Rutherford |first1=Susan |last2=Wan |first2=Justin S.H. |last3=Cohen |first3=Joel M. |last4=Benson |first4=Doug |last5=Rossetto |first5=Maurizio |title=Looks can be deceiving: speciation dynamics of co-distributed ''Angophora'' (Myrtaceae) species in a varying landscape |journal=Evolution |date=February 2021 |volume=75 |issue=2 |pages=310–329 |doi=10.1111/evo.14140|pmid=33325041 |bibcode=2021Evolu..75..310R |s2cid=229281038 }} The Charmhaven apple (''[[Angophora inopina]]'') from the vicinity of [[Wyee]] on the Central Coast of New South Wales is closely related and may be a dwarf form of ''A. floribunda''. ==Distribution and habitat== The range is across eastern Australia, from [[Rolleston, Queensland|Rolleston]] and [[Roma, Queensland|Roma]] in central Queensland though eastern and central New South Wales and into eastern Victoria, where it is found at Mallacoota.{{cite web |title=''Angophora floribunda'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/angophora_floribunda.htm |publisher=Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=5 June 2020}} It is found on alluvial soils, generally on shale or basalt soils. In open forest, it is associated with such trees as swamp she-oak (''[[Casuarina glauca]]''), white stringybark (''[[Eucalyptus globoidea]]''), blackbutt (''[[Eucalyptus pilularis|E. pilularis]]''), Blakelys red gum (''[[Eucalyptus blakelyi|E. blakelyi]]''), forest red gum (''[[Eucalyptus tereticornis|E. tereticornis]]''), brittle gum (''[[Eucalyptus mannifera|E. mannifera]]''), forest she-oak (''[[Allocasuarina torulosa]]''), grey gum (''[[Eucalyptus punctata|E. punctata]]''), and broad-leaved white mahogany (''[[Eucalyptus umbra|E. umbra]]''). In wetter forest, it grows alongside Sydney blue gum (''[[Eucalyptus saligna|E. saligna]]'') and in closed forest alongside lillypilly (''[[Syzygium smithii]]''), cheese tree (''[[Glochidion ferdinandi]]''), Australian white birch (''[[Schizomeria ovata]]'') and sandpaper fig (''[[Ficus coronata]]'') and under emergent specimens of bangalay (''[[Eucalyptus botryoides|E. botryoides]]''), grey ironbark (''[[Eucalyptus paniculata|E. paniculata]]'') and turpentine (''[[Syncarpia glomulifera]]''). ==Ecology== The rough-barked apple regenerates by regrowing from [[epicormic bud]]s after bushfire. Trees live for more than a hundred years. The [[grey-headed flying fox]] (''Pteropus poliocephalus'') and [[little red flying fox]] (''P. scapulatus'') eat the flowers, and the [[white-plumed honeyeater]] (''Ptilotula penicillata'') forages among the flowers. The tree is used as a nesting site by the rare [[regent honeyeater]] (''Anthochaera phrygia''). The [[Buprestidae|jewel beetle]] species ''[[Curis caloptera]]'', ''[[Stigmodera andersoni]]'', ''[[Stigmodera terminatis|S. terminatis]]'' and ''[[Stigmodera vigilans|S. vigilans]]'' also visit the flowers, the latter three species being fairly specific in their preference for ''Angophora floribunda''.{{cite journal|last=Hawkeswood |first=Trevor J. |year=1978 |title=Observations on some Buprestidae (Coleoptera) from the Blue Mountains, N.S.W. |journal=Australian Zoologist |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=257–76 |url=http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/5.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131230235213/http://www.calodema.com/freefiles/5.pdf |archive-date=2013-12-30 }} The [[longhorn beetle]] species ''[[Paroplites australis]]'' and ''[[Agrianome spinicollis]]'' have been recorded from the rough-barked apple.{{cite journal|last=Hawkeswood |first=Trevor J. |year=1992 |title=Review of the biology, host plants and immature stages of the Australian Cerambycidae (Coleoptera). Part 1, Parandrinae and Prioninae |journal=Giornale Italiano di Entomologia |volume=6 |pages=207–24 |url=http://www.cerambycoidea.com/titles/hawskeswood160.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229112927/http://www.cerambycoidea.com/titles/hawskeswood160.pdf |archive-date=2010-12-29 }} ''Angophora floribunda'' has been recorded as a host for several mistletoe species: ''[[Amyema bifurcata]]'', ''[[Amyema miquelii|A. miquelii]]'', ''[[Amyema pendula|A. pendula]]'', ''[[Dendrophthoe curvata]]'', ''[[Dendrophthoe glabrescens|D. glabrescens]]'', ''[[Dendrophthoe vitellina|D. vitellina]]'', ''[[Muellerina celastroides]]'' and ''[[Muellerina eucalyptoides|M. eucalyptoides]]''.{{cite journal|last=Downey|first=Paul O.|year=1998|title=An inventory of host species for each aerial mistletoe species (Loranthaceae and Viscaceae) in Australia|journal=Cunninghamia|volume=5|issue=3|pages=685–720|url=https://www.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/58041/Cun5Dow685.pdf}} Female [[scarlet myzomela]]s (''Myzomela sanguinolenta'') have been observed tearing off bark to use in building their nests.{{cite book |title=[[Handbook of Australian, New Zealand and Antarctic Birds]]. Volume 5: Tyrant-flycatchers to Chats|editor=Higgins, Peter J.|editor2=Peter, Jeffrey M.|editor3=Steele, W. K. |year=2001 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Melbourne |isbn=0-19-553258-9 | page=1169}} ==Cultivation== This is a large plant generally unsuitable for any but the largest gardens. ==Gallery== {{gallery |title=Features of the rough-barked apple (''Angophora floribunda'') |align=center |width=120 |height=120 |style=text-align:center |File:Angophora floribunda foliage.jpg|Foliage |File:Angophora floribunda - adult leaves 01.jpg|Adult leaves |File:Angophora floribunda - fruit.jpg|Fruit |File:Angophora floribunda - inflorescence.jpg|Inflorescence |File:Angophora floribunda - trunk bark.jpg|Trunk bark |File:Angophora floribunda - upper branch bark.jpg|Upper branch bark }} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q3917215}} [[Category:Angophora|floribunda]] [[Category:Flora of New South Wales]] [[Category:Flora of Queensland]] [[Category:Flora of Victoria (state)]] [[Category:Trees of Australia]] [[Category:Ornamental trees]] [[Category:Plants described in 1797]]
